routes.description: Defend divine simplicity as the denial of real intrinsic composition by grounding it in divine aseity and pure actuality, then show that analogous predication, subsistent Trinitarian relations, and extrinsic contingent relations preserve the doctrines named in the motion.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the pro side justifies excluding intrinsic composition from God and supplies coherent accounts of divine attributes, Trinitarian distinctions, freedom in creation, and knowledge of contingent reality without introducing intrinsic potency or change.

motionBridge.description: Establish that the absence of real intrinsic composition can coexist with classical theism, the Trinity, divine freedom, and omniscient knowledge of contingent reality.

centralBridges.description: Derive the exclusion of intrinsic composition from divine aseity or pure actuality by explaining why intrinsic parts would introduce dependence or potency.
Account for real personal distinction through opposed subsistent relations identified with the divine essence rather than through additional intrinsic items.
Locate variation in contingent truths and creature-directed knowledge in extrinsic relations while preserving an unchanging intrinsic divine intellect and causal efficacy.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Explain how diverse divine predicates can signify distinct perfections analogically without requiring distinct intrinsic properties in God.
Explain why a perfect and self-sufficient God may freely create or refrain from creating without acquiring goodness or undergoing intrinsic alteration.

routes.description: Challenge divine simplicity by fixing its strong identity requirements and arguing that Trinitarian processions and omniscient awareness of contingent reality require positive intrinsic distinctions, accidents, potency, or change that simplicity excludes.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the con side shows that at least one indispensable commitment of the stated classical framework—Trinitarian distinction, divine freedom, or contingent omniscience—requires intrinsic differentiation or potentiality inconsistent with the proposed absence of composition.

motionBridge.description: Establish that divine simplicity cannot jointly preserve all of the classical, Trinitarian, freedom, and contingent-knowledge commitments specified by the motion.

centralBridges.description: Define the prohibited composition broadly enough to include any positive ontological item intrinsic to but distinct from God, and test the pro account against that criterion.
Show that asymmetric processions or begottenness constitute positive intrinsic distinctions that cannot all be strictly identical with the undifferentiated Godhead.
Argue that omniscient knowledge across differing contingent realities requires an intrinsic contingent component, acquisition or loss, and therefore potency or change in God.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Block the inference from aseity to simplicity by distinguishing explanatory dependence, self-grounding proposals, and dependence upon realities external to God.
Require an account of what creature-specific divine knowledge consists in if every difference between contingent items of knowledge is assigned wholly outside God.

sections.title: Composition, Aseity, and Pure Actuality
sections.rationale: This issue fixes the operative meaning of intrinsic composition and tests the principal positive inferences from divine independence and pure actuality to simplicity.

sections.title: Divine Attributes, Identity, and Predication
sections.rationale: The coherence of identifying God's being, power, knowledge, love, and other perfections depends on whether conceptual, analogical, or truthmaker distinctions can sustain diverse true predications without intrinsic parts.

sections.title: Trinitarian Persons, Processions, and Relations
sections.rationale: The motion expressly requires compatibility with Trinitarian doctrine, making the status of subsistent relations, asymmetric processions, and personal distinction an independent burden-bearing issue.

sections.title: Omniscience and the Intrinsic–Extrinsic Divide
sections.rationale: The dispute over knowledge in an alone world and across changing creaturely realities tests whether contingent omniscience introduces an intrinsic accident or can instead vary through extrinsic truth conditions.

sections.title: Divine Freedom, Change, and Potentiality
sections.rationale: Whether God may create or refrain from creating, acquire or lose knowledge predicates, and remain immutable determines whether simplicity is compatible with contingent creation and free divine action.
